A measure of the density of connections in a graph. A combinatorial analogue of Ricci curvature from differential geometry, used to study local connectivity and geometry of graphs. A measure of the shortest path length. A measure of the number of cycles.

491 What is the "topological phase transition" in physics?

A phase transition that is driven by changes in temperature. A phase transition where the topological order of a system changes, often without breaking any local symmetries. A phase transition that involves changes in volume. A phase transition that changes the material's color.

492 What is a "topological quantum computer"?

A quantum computer that uses classical bits. A theoretical quantum computer that stores and processes information using topological properties of exotic states of matter, offering robust computation. A computer that is very large. A computer that uses only topological data.

493 What is a "topological defect" in physics?

An error in a material's structure. A stable, localized disturbance in a physical system (e.g., crystal, field theory) that cannot be removed by local smooth deformations, classified by topological invariants. A weak point in a material. A defect that can be easily repaired.

494 What is a "topological entropy" in data analysis?

A measure of data redundancy. A measure of the complexity or information content of a data set, related to the growth rate of distinguishable patterns. A measure of data randomness. A measure of data size.

495 What is the "interleaving distance" for persistent modules?

A metric that measures the distance between two persistent modules, important for the stability theorems in persistent homology. A distance measure for two data points. A distance measure for two graphs. A distance measure for two topological spaces.

496 What is the "computational complexity" of homology computation?

Always constant time. Typically polynomial in the number of simplices, but can be exponential in dimension for some cases. Always linear time. Independent of the size of the complex.

497 What is "computational knot theory"?

The use of algorithms to study and classify knots and links. The manual classification of knots. The study of the physical properties of ropes. The creation of new knot diagrams.

498 What is the "Knot Atlas"?

A book about knots. A mathematical database and online resource providing information and invariants for a large number of knots and links. A map of places where knots are found. A tool for tying knots.

499 What is "visual computing" in combinatorial topology?

The use of computer graphics and visualization techniques to understand and explore topological structures and concepts. The study of human vision. The development of new algorithms for computation. The use of physical models to demonstrate topology.

102 What is 'Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) test'?

A non-parametric alternative to ANOVA. A post-hoc test used after ANOVA to perform all pairwise comparisons between group means while controlling the family-wise error rate. A test for homogeneity of variances. A method for calculating the overall effect size in ANOVA.

103 What is the principle behind 'Fiducial Inference'?

It is a strictly Bayesian approach to inference. It attempts to directly construct a probability distribution for a parameter without a prior, based solely on the observed data and the model. It only uses point estimates for parameters. It is a resampling method like bootstrapping.

104 What is the 'Delta method' used for in statistics?

To perform exact hypothesis tests. To approximate the sampling distribution (and thus variance and standard error) of a function of an estimator. To calculate confidence intervals for proportions. To compare the means of two large samples.

105 What does 'blocking' in experimental design aim to achieve?

To increase the number of treatments in an experiment. To reduce the variability within experimental units by grouping similar units together, thereby improving the precision of treatment effect estimates. To ensure all participants receive the placebo. To introduce intentional bias to test a specific theory.

106 What is the 'Cramér-Rao lower bound' in estimation theory?

The maximum possible variance an estimator can have. The theoretical minimum variance that any unbiased estimator of a parameter can achieve. The smallest sample size required for an unbiased estimator. A measure of the bias of an estimator.

107 What is the 'likelihood principle' in statistical inference?

It states that prior distributions are more important than the data. It states that all relevant information from an experiment regarding unknown parameters is contained in the likelihood function. It implies that only large sample sizes lead to valid inferences. It requires the use of a normal distribution for all data.

108 What is 'Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE)' primarily used for?

Analyzing independent observations with a normal distribution. Analyzing longitudinal or clustered data by accounting for the correlation structure within clusters, especially when the focus is on population-averaged effects. Fitting linear models with multiple continuous predictors. Performing non-parametric tests on small samples.

109 What is 'information theory' and its relevance to statistics?

It is a branch of computer science focused on data storage. It provides a mathematical framework for quantifying information, uncertainty, and entropy, which is used in areas like model selection (AIC, BIC) and machine learning. It is concerned with the efficient collection of data. It only applies to quantum mechanics.

110 What is the role of a 'link function' in Generalized Linear Models (GLMs)?

It connects the predictors to the variance of the response. It specifies the relationship between the linear predictor and the mean of the response variable, allowing for non-normal error distributions. It transforms the independent variables. It handles missing values in the response variable.

111 What is the primary use of 'meta-analysis'?

To conduct a new, large-scale experiment. To systematically synthesize and combine results from multiple independent studies to derive a pooled estimate or draw more robust conclusions. To describe a single large dataset comprehensively. To develop new statistical methodologies.

112 In survival analysis, what does the "hazard ratio" represent?

The ratio of mean survival times between two groups. The ratio of the hazard rates (instantaneous risk of event) between two groups. The difference in survival probabilities at a specific time point. The cumulative incidence of an event.

113 What is 'latent variable modeling'?

A type of regression model for hidden variables. A statistical approach that models relationships between observed variables and unobserved (latent) constructs or factors. A method for dealing with missing data. A technique for time series forecasting.

114 What is 'Granger causality'?

A statistical test that proves cause and effect. A statistical concept that suggests if X "Granger-causes" Y, then past values of X help predict Y better than past values of Y alone. It implies predictability, not true causation. A method for identifying confounders in observational studies. A technique for estimating parameters in structural equation models.

115 What is 'propensity score matching'?

A method for randomizing participants in an experiment. A technique used in observational studies to balance covariates between treatment and control groups by matching subjects based on their estimated propensity scores. A method for dealing with multicollinearity. A way to identify interaction effects.

116 What is 'structural equation modeling (SEM)'?

A statistical method used for simple linear regression. A multivariate statistical analysis technique that combines aspects of factor analysis and multiple regression to test complex causal models involving observed and latent variables. A method for comparing means across many groups. A non-parametric test for categorical data.

117 What is 'sample size determination' and why is it important?

It's the process of randomly selecting participants. It's the calculation of the number of subjects required to detect an effect of a given size with a specified level of power and significance, crucial for ethical and efficient research. It determines the representativeness of a sample. It ensures data are normally distributed.

118 What is 'cross-sectional data'?

Data collected on a single unit over multiple time periods. Data collected on multiple units at a single point in time. Data collected from a randomized controlled trial. Data that is non-normally distributed.

119 What is 'panel data' (or longitudinal data)?

Data collected on multiple units at a single point in time. Data collected on a single unit over multiple time periods. Data collected on multiple units over multiple time periods. Data that is purely qualitative.

120 What is the 'ecological fallacy'?

Drawing conclusions about individuals based on data aggregated at a group level. Drawing conclusions about groups based on data from individuals. The error of using too small a sample size. The mistake of assuming correlation implies causation.

121 What is 'Simpson's Paradox'?

A paradox where a trend appears in several different groups of data but disappears or reverses when these groups are combined. A statistical paradox related to the central limit theorem. A problem that arises in multiple regression with multicollinearity. A paradox related to the non-identifiability of model parameters.

122 What is 'surrogate endpoint' in clinical trials?

A primary outcome that is directly measured. A measure that substitutes for a clinical endpoint of interest, often used because the clinical endpoint is too far in the future or difficult to measure. An adverse event in a clinical trial. A secondary outcome that confirms the primary finding.

123 What is 'data imputation'?

The process of collecting new data to fill gaps. The process of replacing missing data with substituted values. The process of transforming data to achieve normality. The process of removing outliers from a dataset.

124 What is 'multiple imputation'?

A single method for replacing all missing values. A technique where missing values are replaced multiple times, creating several complete datasets, which are then analyzed and combined for more robust estimates and standard errors. A method for imputing categorical variables only. A method that only works for ignorable missingness.

125 What is the 'Hotelling's T-squared statistic'?

A univariate test for comparing two means. A multivariate generalization of Student's t-test, used to test hypotheses about the means of two or more related groups or variables. A non-parametric test for comparing distributions. A test for homogeneity of variances.

126 What is 'MANOVA' (Multivariate Analysis of Variance)?

A technique for comparing means on a single dependent variable across multiple groups. A statistical test used to compare the means of two or more groups on two or more dependent variables simultaneously. A regression technique for multivariate outcomes. A non-parametric test for multiple comparisons.

127 What is 'Discriminant Analysis'?

A technique for predicting a continuous dependent variable. A statistical technique used to classify observations into one of several predefined groups based on a set of predictor variables. A method for reducing the dimensionality of data. A technique for identifying causal relationships.

128 What is 'Cluster Analysis'?

A supervised learning technique for classification. An unsupervised learning technique used to group a set of objects in such a way that objects in the same group (cluster) are more similar to each other than to those in other groups. A method for predicting future values in a time series. A technique for testing hypotheses about means.

129 What is 'item response theory (IRT)'?

A theory for analyzing economic data. A psychometric theory that models the relationship between an individual's latent trait (e.g., ability, attitude) and their responses to test items. A theory for designing randomized controlled trials. A method for calculating correlation coefficients.

130 What is the 'Rao-Blackwell theorem' in estimation theory?

It states that the sample mean is an unbiased estimator. It states that if an unbiased estimator exists, it is possible to improve it by conditioning on a sufficient statistic, resulting in an estimator with smaller variance. It provides the lower bound for the variance of any estimator. It defines the conditions for consistency of an estimator.

131 What is 'information matrix' in maximum likelihood estimation?

A matrix of all observed data points. A matrix containing information about the second derivatives of the log-likelihood function, whose inverse often approximates the covariance matrix of the MLEs. A matrix used to check for multicollinearity. A matrix for transforming variables.

132 What is 'score test' (or Rao's score test) in hypothesis testing?

A test that compares the restricted and unrestricted likelihoods. A test that uses the score function (gradient of the log-likelihood) evaluated under the null hypothesis to test parameter restrictions, often useful when the full model cannot be easily estimated. A test that directly compares the parameter estimates to zero. A test for non-normal errors.

133 What is 'deviance' in Generalized Linear Models (GLMs)?

A measure of the dispersion of the residuals. A generalization of the sum of squares of residuals, used as a measure of the fit of a model and for comparing nested models. The difference between observed and predicted values. The number of outliers in the dataset.

134 What is 'concordance index (C-index)'?

A measure of correlation for categorical variables. A measure of the predictive accuracy of survival models, indicating the proportion of all comparable pairs of subjects for whom the predictions are in agreement with the actual outcomes. A metric for assessing linearity in regression. A measure of consistency between two raters.

135 What is 'copula function' in multivariate statistics?

A function used to model linear relationships between variables. A function that joins multivariate cumulative distribution functions to their one-dimensional marginal distribution functions, useful for modeling dependence structures. A function used to transform data to normality. A function for estimating parameters in time series models.

136 What is 'causal mediation analysis'?

A method for studying direct causal effects only. A statistical approach that investigates the extent to which an intervention or exposure affects an outcome through one or more intermediate variables (mediators). A technique for identifying confounders in observational studies. A method for performing randomized experiments.

137 What is 'Average Treatment Effect (ATE)'?

The effect of a treatment on a specific individual. The average difference in potential outcomes (e.g., outcome with treatment vs. outcome without treatment) across an entire population. The effect of a placebo in a control group. The maximum possible effect of a treatment.

138 What is 'Instrumental Variable (IV)'?

A variable that is directly affected by the treatment. A variable that is correlated with the endogenous independent variable but not directly with the dependent variable, and affects the dependent variable only through the endogenous variable. A variable that controls for confounding. A variable that is always randomized.

139 What is 'heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE)'?

The uniform effect of a treatment across all individuals. The variation in the causal effect of a treatment across different individuals or subgroups within a population. The difference between treatment and control group means. A problem of unequal variances in an experiment.

140 What is 'Synthetic Control Method'?

A method for comparing two randomized groups. A statistical method used in comparative case studies to estimate the effect of an intervention by constructing a "synthetic" control group as a weighted average of unexposed units. A technique for creating simulated data. A method for reducing the dimensionality of panel data.

141 What is 'Confounder' in causal inference?

A variable that is only affected by the treatment. A variable that influences both the treatment assignment and the outcome, and is not an intermediate step in the causal pathway, thus distorting the estimated effect if not accounted for. A variable that is measured after the outcome. A variable that is always randomized out.

142 What is 'Collider' in causal inference?

A variable that causes both the treatment and the outcome. A variable that is a common effect of two or more other variables, and conditioning on it can induce spurious associations between its causes. A variable that mediates the effect between two others. A variable that is always irrelevant to the causal question.

143 What is 'Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) for d-separation'?

A method for identifying which variables are correlated. A graphical criterion used in DAGs to determine if two sets of variables are conditionally independent, given a third set of variables, which is fundamental for identifying confounding and valid adjustment sets. A technique for drawing causal diagrams. A statistical test for conditional independence.

144 What is 'Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)'?

A non-experimental method that estimates treatment effects by comparing outcomes of individuals just above and just below a cutoff point for treatment assignment. A method that relies on perfect randomization. A technique for analyzing discrete outcomes in regression. A method for studying long-term trends in data.

145 What is 'Difference-in-Differences (DiD) estimator'?

An estimator used only in randomized experiments. A statistical technique that estimates the effect of a treatment or intervention by comparing the change in outcomes over time between a treatment group and a control group. A method for comparing two means at a single time point. A technique for analyzing stationary time series.

146 What is 'Fixed Effects Model' in panel data analysis?

A model that assumes the unobserved individual-specific effects are uncorrelated with the independent variables. A model that controls for unobserved, time-invariant individual-specific effects by allowing the intercept to vary across individuals but be constant over time for each individual. A model that treats all individual-specific effects as random draws from a distribution. A model that does not account for individual heterogeneity.

147 What is 'Random Effects Model' in panel data analysis?

A model that assumes the unobserved individual-specific effects are correlated with the independent variables. A model that treats the unobserved individual-specific effects as random variables drawn from a distribution, often used when individual effects are believed to be random samples from a larger population. A model that only considers time-variant covariates. A model that ignores individual heterogeneity.

148 What is 'Mendelian Randomization'?

A method for randomly assigning interventions in clinical trials. A method using genetic variants as instrumental variables to infer causal relationships between risk factors and disease outcomes, reducing confounding and reverse causation. A statistical test for genetic associations. A technique for imputing missing genetic data.

149 What is 'Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA)'?

A method for selecting a single best model from a set of candidates. A technique that combines predictions from multiple models, weighted by their posterior probabilities, to account for model uncertainty and improve predictive performance. A method for fitting models with specific prior distributions. A method for identifying outliers in complex models.

Statistics: insights from numerical data.

1 Which branch of statistics focuses on describing the main features of a dataset?

Inferential statistics Descriptive statistics Predictive statistics Experimental statistics

2 What is the least appropriate measure of central tendency for a highly skewed distribution?

Median Mode Mean Quartile

3 For categorical data, which measure of central tendency is most appropriate?

Mean Median Mode Range

4 What is the term for a graphical representation that summarizes data using five key values: minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum?

Histogram Bar chart Box plot Scatter plot

5 What is the difference between quantitative and qualitative data?

Quantitative data is always discrete, qualitative is always continuous. Quantitative data is numerical, qualitative data is categorical. Quantitative data is subjective, qualitative data is objective. Quantitative data is for populations, qualitative data is for samples.

6 Which measure of dispersion is calculated by taking the average of the squared differences from the mean?

Standard deviation Range Variance Interquartile range

7 What does a population parameter refer to?

A characteristic of a sample. A numerical characteristic of a population. A statistic used to estimate a sample characteristic. A variable collected in an experiment.

8 What is the symbol typically used to represent the population mean?

$\bar{x}$ s μ p

9 Which type of probability is based on observations from experiments or historical data?

Theoretical probability Subjective probability Empirical probability Axiomatic probability

10 If two events are independent, what does this mean about their occurrence?

They cannot happen at the same time. The occurrence of one affects the probability of the other. The occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other. They always happen together.

11 What is the primary purpose of inferential statistics?

To summarize characteristics of a sample. To describe data visually. To make generalizations about a population based on sample data. To cleanse and organize raw data.

12 What is the alternative hypothesis (H₁) in hypothesis testing?

A statement of no effect or no difference. A statement that contradicts the null hypothesis, suggesting an effect or difference. The hypothesis that is always assumed to be true. A hypothesis that only applies to the sample.

13 What does a P-value greater than the significance level (α) typically lead to in hypothesis testing?

Rejecting the null hypothesis. Failing to reject the null hypothesis. Accepting the alternative hypothesis. Increasing the sample size.

14 What is a Type II error?

Rejecting a true null hypothesis. Failing to reject a false null hypothesis. Incorrectly accepting a true alternative hypothesis. Making a calculation error in the test statistic.

15 What is the critical value in hypothesis testing?

The probability of observing the data given the null hypothesis. The boundary that determines whether the null hypothesis should be rejected. The calculated value of the test statistic. The sample mean.

16 Which of the following is an assumption of the independent samples t-test?

The dependent variable is categorical. The samples are dependent. The population variances are equal (homoscedasticity). The sample sizes are always equal.

17 What is the coefficient of determination (R²) used for in linear regression?

To determine the slope of the regression line. To measure the strength and direction of the linear relationship. To assess the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable(s). To calculate the p-value of the regression model.

18 What is an experimental study design characterized by?

Researchers observing phenomena without intervention. Manipulation of an independent variable and random assignment to groups. Relying on historical data only. Primarily collecting qualitative data.

19 What is the purpose of randomization in experimental design?

To make the study easier to conduct. To ensure all participants are treated equally. To minimize bias and ensure groups are comparable, on average, at baseline. To increase the power of the statistical tests.

20 What is a confounding variable?

A variable that is directly manipulated by the researcher. A variable that is an outcome of interest. A variable that affects both the independent and dependent variables, potentially creating a spurious association. A variable that moderates the relationship between two other variables.

21 When would you typically use a one-way ANOVA?

To compare two population means. To compare the means of two or more independent groups on a single continuous dependent variable. To analyze the relationship between two categorical variables. To predict a continuous variable from another continuous variable.

22 What is a post-hoc test used for after a significant ANOVA result?

To increase the overall significance of the ANOVA. To identify which specific group means differ from each other. To check the assumptions of the ANOVA. To recalculate the F-statistic.

23 What does the term "statistical power" refer to?

The probability of making a Type I error. The probability of making a Type II error. The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. The strength of the observed effect.

24 What is the primary use of a Z-score?

To calculate the mean of a dataset. To describe how far a data point is from the mean in terms of standard deviations. To determine the mode of a distribution. To find the interquartile range.

25 What is the Central Limit Theorem's implication for sampling distributions?

All populations are normally distributed. The sampling distribution of the sample mean will be exactly normal for any sample size. For large sample sizes, the sampling distribution of the sample mean will be approximately normal, regardless of the population distribution. The sample mean will always equal the population mean.

26 What is the primary characteristic of a normal distribution?

It is always skewed to the right. It is perfectly symmetrical and bell-shaped. It has multiple modes. Its mean is always zero.

27 What is a uniform probability distribution?

A distribution where probabilities are concentrated at the center. A distribution where all outcomes have an equal probability of occurring. A distribution that is highly skewed. A distribution where the mean, median, and mode are all different.

28 What is the expected value of a discrete random variable?

The value that has the highest probability. The most extreme value in the distribution. The long-run average of the outcomes if the experiment were repeated many times. The standard deviation of the variable.

29 Which probability distribution models the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space, given a constant average rate?

Binomial distribution Normal distribution Poisson distribution Uniform distribution

30 What is a confidence interval's purpose?

To provide a single best estimate of a population parameter. To give a range of plausible values for a population parameter, along with a confidence level. To determine the statistical significance of a hypothesis test. To visualize the spread of data.

31 What is the primary use of a Chi-Square goodness-of-fit test?

To compare the means of two groups. To test if observed categorical data fit an expected distribution. To test for a linear relationship between two continuous variables. To predict a dependent variable from an independent variable.

32 What is a non-parametric test?

A statistical test that makes strong assumptions about the population distribution (e.g., normality). A statistical test that does not require specific assumptions about the population distribution. A test that is only used for very large sample sizes. A test that only works for categorical data.

33 When is the Mann-Whitney U test appropriate?

As a parametric alternative to ANOVA. As a non-parametric alternative to the independent samples t-test for comparing two independent groups. As an alternative to the paired t-test. For comparing more than two independent groups.

34 What does a high correlation coefficient (close to 1 or -1) indicate?

A weak linear relationship. A strong linear relationship. No linear relationship. A causal relationship.

35 What is the primary difference between correlation and causation?

Correlation implies one variable directly affects another, causation implies only an association. Correlation measures the strength of association, causation implies one variable causes another. Causation is for quantitative variables, correlation is for qualitative. Correlation is always linear, causation can be non-linear.

36 What are residuals in a regression model?

The predicted values of the dependent variable. The differences between the observed values and the predicted values of the dependent variable. The values of the independent variable. The regression coefficients.

37 What is heteroscedasticity in linear regression?

The error terms are correlated. The variance of the error terms is not constant across all levels of the independent variable. The independent variables are highly correlated. The error terms are not normally distributed.

38 What is the purpose of conducting a power analysis before a study?

To determine the statistical significance level. To calculate the minimum sample size needed to detect an effect of a given size with a specified probability (power). To estimate the effect size of the intervention. To perform a preliminary hypothesis test.

39 What is a convenience sample?

A sample selected using a random number generator. A sample where individuals are chosen based on their easy accessibility. A sample where the population is divided into subgroups, and then individuals are randomly selected from each subgroup. A sample where every nth individual is selected.

40 What is the ethical principle of "informed consent" in research?

Participants must be fully aware of the study's purpose, risks, and benefits before agreeing to participate. Researchers must only recruit participants who are fully informed about statistics. Data collected must always be made public. Researchers must inform participants of the study's exact hypotheses upfront.

41 What is the definition of a statistic?

A numerical measure that describes a characteristic of a population. A numerical measure that describes a characteristic of a sample. A statement about the relationship between two variables. A qualitative description of a dataset.

42 What is the purpose of a stem-and-leaf plot?

To display the relationship between two quantitative variables. To show the proportion of categories within a whole. To organize numerical data and show its shape and distribution while preserving individual data values. To compare means of different groups.

43 What is the formula for the standard error of the mean?

Standard deviation / Sample size Variance / Sample size Standard deviation / sqrt(Sample size) Mean / Standard deviation

44 What is the primary characteristic of an ordinal variable?

Categories without order (e.g., eye color). Categories with a meaningful order but unequal intervals (e.g., education level). Numerical values with meaningful differences and a true zero (e.g., height). Numerical values with meaningful differences but no true zero (e.g., temperature in Celsius).

45 What is the purpose of ANOVA's F-statistic?

To compare two individual means. To test whether there are significant differences between the means of two or more groups. To measure the strength of association between two categorical variables. To determine the correlation between two continuous variables.

46 What does the term "degrees of freedom" generally indicate in statistical tests?

The total number of observations. The number of parameters estimated from the data. The number of independent values or observations that are free to vary in a calculation or model. The number of variables included in the analysis.

47 What is the main difference between a P-value and a confidence interval?

P-values indicate effect size, confidence intervals indicate significance. P-values test a specific hypothesis, confidence intervals provide a range of plausible values for a parameter. P-values are for parametric tests, confidence intervals are for non-parametric. Confidence intervals are always narrower than P-values.

48 What is a potential issue with using the mean for skewed data?

It becomes identical to the median. It is pulled towards the longer tail, misrepresenting the typical value. It becomes zero. It is undefined.

49 What is the difference between a one-tailed and a two-tailed hypothesis test?

A one-tailed test has a smaller sample size. A one-tailed test specifies a direction for the effect, while a two-tailed test looks for a difference in either direction. A two-tailed test is always more powerful. A one-tailed test is only used when there is no prior expectation.

50 What is a quasi-experimental design?

A design that involves random assignment to treatment and control groups. A design that attempts to establish a cause-and-effect relationship but lacks full random assignment. A purely observational study. A design that only collects qualitative data.

51 What is 'multicollinearity' in multiple regression?

When the residuals are not normally distributed. When two or more independent variables in the model are highly correlated with each other. When the dependent variable is highly correlated with an independent variable. When the relationship between variables is non-linear.

52 What does the 'effect size' measure in a statistical test?

The probability of the null hypothesis being true. The strength or magnitude of the observed relationship or difference. The P-value of the test. The sample size of the study.

53 What is 'bootstrapping' in statistical inference?

A method for conducting exact hypothesis tests on small samples. A resampling technique used to estimate the sampling distribution of a statistic or to construct confidence intervals without strong distributional assumptions. A method for reducing the number of parameters in a model. A technique for handling missing data.

54 What is the primary purpose of 'Principal Component Analysis (PCA)'?

To predict a dependent variable. To reduce the dimensionality of a dataset by transforming a set of possibly correlated variables into a smaller set of uncorrelated components. To cluster observations into groups. To test hypotheses about means.

55 What is 'Bayesian inference'?

A statistical approach that relies solely on p-values to make decisions. A statistical approach that updates prior beliefs about parameters using observed data to produce posterior probabilities. A method for calculating exact confidence intervals. A purely descriptive statistical method.

56 What is 'maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)'?

A method for minimizing the sum of squared errors. A method for finding the parameter values that make the observed data most probable. A method for calculating posterior probabilities. A method for hypothesis testing without distributional assumptions.

57 What is a 'Generalized Linear Model (GLM)'?

A model that only applies to normally distributed data. An extension of linear regression that allows for response variables with error distribution models other than a normal distribution and uses a link function to relate the mean of the response to the linear predictor. A model used exclusively for time series data. A non-parametric regression technique.

58 What is the role of a 'link function' in GLMs?

To transform the independent variables to be linear. To connect the linear predictor (combination of covariates) to the expected value of the response variable. To specify the distribution of the error term. To handle missing values in the dataset.

59 What is 'cross-validation' used for in machine learning and statistics?

To increase the complexity of a model. To assess how well a model will generalize to an independent dataset and to prevent overfitting. To reduce multicollinearity. To transform non-linear relationships into linear ones.

60 What is the 'bias-variance trade-off'?

The trade-off between making a Type I and Type II error. The conflict in model building where a simple model has high bias and low variance, while a complex model has low bias and high variance, and the goal is to find an optimal balance. The choice between parametric and non-parametric tests. The balance between statistical significance and practical significance.

61 What is 'Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)' primarily used for?

To calculate exact analytical solutions for complex integrals. To simulate samples from complex probability distributions, especially posterior distributions in Bayesian inference, when direct computation is intractable. To perform frequentist hypothesis tests. To optimize likelihood functions in maximum likelihood estimation.

62 What is 'time series analysis' concerned with?

Analyzing data collected at a single point in time. Analyzing data collected over time, identifying patterns, trends, and seasonality. Analyzing relationships between categorical variables. Analyzing spatial data.

63 What is 'Kaplan-Meier estimator' used for?

To estimate the mean of non-normal data. To estimate the survival function (probability of surviving beyond a certain time) from time-to-event data. To conduct hypothesis tests for categorical data. To model complex non-linear relationships in regression.

64 What is the primary purpose of 'meta-analysis'?

To conduct a new experiment with a larger sample size. To systematically combine and analyze results from multiple independent studies to derive a pooled estimate or synthesize evidence. To describe the characteristics of a single large dataset. To develop new statistical methods.

65 What does 'robustness' imply about a statistical method?

It is computationally fast. It is highly accurate even with small samples. It is relatively insensitive to minor violations of its underlying assumptions. It always yields statistically significant results.

66 What is an 'interaction effect' in ANOVA or regression?

The independent effect of one variable on the dependent variable. The effect of one independent variable on the dependent variable changes depending on the level of another independent variable. The correlation between two independent variables. The error term in the model.

67 What is the 'curse of dimensionality'?

The difficulty of visualizing 3D data. The phenomenon where the volume of the data space increases exponentially with the number of dimensions, making data sparse and analyses difficult without significantly more data. The problem of multicollinearity in high-dimensional regression. The challenge of interpreting simple linear models.

68 What is 'Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve' used for?

To assess the linearity of a regression model. To evaluate the performance of a binary classifier system across different discrimination thresholds. To compare the means of multiple groups. To visualize correlations between multiple variables.

69 What is a 'prior distribution' in Bayesian statistics?

The distribution of observed data before analysis. The probability distribution representing existing beliefs about a parameter before new data are incorporated. The distribution of residuals in a model. The sampling distribution of a statistic.

70 What is a 'posterior distribution' in Bayesian statistics?

The distribution of data collected after the experiment. The updated probability distribution of a parameter, reflecting revised beliefs after incorporating new data. The distribution of the null hypothesis. The distribution of predicted values.

71 What is 'propensity score matching'?

A method for randomizing participants in observational studies. A technique used in observational studies to balance covariates between treatment and control groups by matching subjects based on their estimated propensity scores. A method for dealing with multicollinearity. A way to identify interaction effects.

72 What is 'instrumental variables (IV) regression'?

A method for dealing with multicollinearity. A technique used to address endogeneity (correlation between an independent variable and the error term) by using an instrumental variable that affects the outcome only through the endogenous variable. A method for standardizing independent variables. A technique for fitting non-linear models.

73 What is 'kernel density estimate (KDE)'?

A method for calculating correlation. A non-parametric way to estimate the probability density function of a random variable, smoothing observed data points. A technique for reducing the dimensionality of data. A method for clustering data points.

74 What is 'regularization' in statistical learning?

A method to ensure the data is normally distributed. A technique to prevent overfitting and improve model generalization by adding a penalty to the loss function based on the size of model coefficients. A process to standardize features. A way to transform categorical variables into numerical ones.

75 What is 'factor analysis'?

76 What does 'identifiability' mean for statistical models?

77 What are 'robust standard errors' (e.g., Huber-White standard errors) used for?

78 What is a 'Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)' used for in causal inference?

79 What is 'Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation' in Bayesian statistics?

1 What is the primary characteristic of a Uniformly Most Powerful (UMP) test in hypothesis testing?

5 In the context of Generalised Linear Models (GLMs), what function relates the expected value of the response variable to the linear predictor?

9 What constitutes a "non-informative prior" in Bayesian statistics, and what is a common example?

A prior that reflects strong subjective beliefs, like a very narrow normal distribution. A prior that exerts minimal influence on the posterior, allowing data to dominate, such as a Jeffreys prior. A prior that leads to an analytical solution for the posterior distribution. A prior that is always uniform across all parameter values.

10 In causal inference, what does the "ignorability assumption" for treatment assignment entail?

11 What is the primary role of "state-space models" in time series analysis?

To represent a time series by defining an unobserved "state" process and an observed "measurement" process, allowing for filtering and forecasting. To remove seasonal components from a time series. To detect structural breaks in financial time series.

12 What is the "breakdown point" of an estimator, particularly in robust statistics?

The sample size at which the estimator becomes unreliable. The smallest proportion of outliers that can cause an estimator to become arbitrarily biased. The point at which the estimator reaches its maximum efficiency. The number of iterations an algorithm takes to converge.

13 In survival analysis, what phenomenon does a "Cox proportional hazards model" implicitly assume?

14 What is the primary challenge addressed by "Instrumental Variable (IV) regression" in observational studies?

Measurement error in the dependent variable. Multicollinearity among independent variables. Unobserved confounding that biases the estimated causal effect of an endogenous predictor. Non-linear relationships between variables.

15 What defines the concept of "ancillarity" for a statistic in the presence of nuisance parameters?

A statistic whose distribution depends on the parameter of interest. A statistic whose distribution does not depend on the parameter of interest or any nuisance parameters. By directly solving for the parameters using a closed-form solution. By performing a gradient descent optimization on the likelihood function. By simulating posterior distributions using MCMC methods.

To classify observations into distinct groups based on multiple variables. To model the causal relationships among multiple variables using a path diagram.

18 What is the "Dirichlet process" primarily used for in non-parametric Bayesian statistics?

As a prior distribution for a specific parameter of a fixed distribution. As a prior distribution over distributions, allowing for flexible clustering or density estimation without assuming a fixed number of components. To generate samples from a known posterior distribution. To test the goodness-of-fit for a parametric model.

19 What is the main distinction between "weak ignorability" and "strong ignorability" in causal inference?

Strong ignorability implies weak ignorability, with the added condition of common support for propensity scores. Weak ignorability allows for unobserved confounders, while strong ignorability does not. Strong ignorability only applies to randomized controlled trials. Weak ignorability is a less restrictive assumption than strong ignorability, especially regarding treatment assignment conditional on observed covariates.

20 What is the "Anderson-Darling test" primarily used for?

To compare the means of two independent groups. To test whether a sample of data comes from a specified distribution, placing more emphasis on the tails than the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. To assess the association between two categorical variables. To detect autocorrelation in time series residuals.

21 How does "Lasso regression" differ from "Ridge regression" in terms of regularization and variable selection?

Lasso uses an L2 penalty, while Ridge uses an L1 penalty. Lasso tends to shrink some coefficients exactly to zero, performing variable selection, while Ridge shrinks coefficients towards zero but rarely to exactly zero. 22 In time series, what is the primary purpose of an "Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (ARCH)" model?

To model the conditional mean of a time series. To capture the tendency for the volatility of financial time series to cluster over time, where past error magnitudes influence current conditional variance. To remove trends and seasonality from a time series. To predict long-term economic growth.

23 What is the "Hájek-Le Cam convolution theorem" foundational for in asymptotic efficiency?

It establishes the conditions under which an estimator is consistent. It states that no regular estimator can have an asymptotic variance smaller than the inverse of the Fisher information, similar to the CRLB but for asymptotic settings. 24 What is "empirical likelihood" inference, and what is its main advantage?

It is a non-parametric method for constructing confidence intervals by maximizing a likelihood function without assuming a parametric distribution for the data. It is a Bayesian method for combining prior beliefs with observed data. It is a technique for performing exact hypothesis tests for categorical data. It is used for imputing missing values in a dataset.

25 In decision theory, what does the "Minimax principle" seek to achieve?

To minimize the maximum possible loss, ensuring the best outcome in the worst-case scenario. To maximize the expected utility of a decision. To choose the action that has the highest probability of success. To balance Type I and Type II errors perfectly.

26 What is a "quasi-likelihood function" used for in generalized linear models?

To estimate parameters when the exact likelihood function is unknown but the mean-variance relationship is specified. To ensure that the residuals are normally distributed. To perform exact hypothesis tests for count data. To handle non-linear relationships without transforming the data.

27 What is the primary purpose of "Generalized Additive Models (GAMs)" compared to traditional GLMs?

To force all relationships between predictors and the response to be linear. To allow for non-linear relationships by modeling the effect of each predictor with a smooth function (e.g., splines) while maintaining additivity. To include random effects in the model. To handle time-series data with seasonal components.

28 What is the "Savage-Dickey density ratio" used for in Bayesian model comparison?

To calculate the posterior predictive distribution. To compute the Bayes factor by evaluating the ratio of the posterior density to the prior density at the null hypothesis value. To identify the most influential observations in a Bayesian model. To determine the optimal number of components in a mixture model.

29 What is "Fisher Information" a measure of, and what role does it play in estimation theory?

It measures the amount of uncertainty in a parameter estimate. It quantifies the amount of information a random sample contains about an unknown parameter, determining the lower bound for the variance of an unbiased estimator. It describes the correlation between two independent variables. It is an alternative to the p-value for hypothesis testing.

30 What is "de Finetti's Theorem" a cornerstone for in subjective Bayesian probability?

It proves that all sequences of random variables must be independent. It establishes that if one's beliefs about a sequence of random events are exchangeable, then they can be represented as a mixture of independent and identically distributed events conditional on some parameter. It shows that objective probabilities can always be derived from subjective ones. It defines the conditions under which a prior distribution is non-informative.

31 In the context of causal inference, what is the "front-door criterion" for identification?

A condition for identifying the average treatment effect when there are unobserved confounders that affect both treatment and outcome, but whose effect is fully mediated by an observed variable. A method for selecting relevant covariates for propensity score matching. A graphical criterion used in experimental design for optimal randomization. A statistical test for assessing the validity of instrumental variables.

32 What is the purpose of a "generalized linear mixed model (GLMM)"?

To analyze data with a continuous response variable and only fixed effects. To extend GLMs by incorporating random effects, suitable for clustered or longitudinal non-normal data. To fit linear models to time-series data with irregular spacing. To perform non-parametric regression without making any distributional assumptions.

33 What does "co-integration" signify in time series econometrics?

That two or more time series are stationary. That two or more non-stationary time series have a long-run equilibrium relationship, even if they individually trend over time. That all time series in a system are perfectly uncorrelated. That the residuals from a regression of two time series are always white noise.

34 How do "M-estimators" (e.g., in robust regression) address the influence of outliers?

By giving equal weight to all observations regardless of their residual size. By down-weighting observations with large residuals, thereby making the estimator less sensitive to outliers. By removing outliers from the dataset before estimation. By transforming the data to achieve normality.

35 What is the fundamental idea behind "Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)" methods in Bayesian statistics?

To directly compute complex posterior distributions analytically. To construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the desired posterior distribution, allowing for sampling from it when direct computation is infeasible. To perform maximum likelihood estimation for models with many parameters. To approximate p-values for non-parametric tests.

36 What is "Stein's Paradox" or the "Marginalization Paradox" in estimation?

The observation that a sample mean is always a biased estimator of the population mean. The counterintuitive finding that combining estimates of distinct parameters, even seemingly unrelated ones, can lead to uniformly better estimates for each parameter, especially for higher dimensions. The phenomenon where adding more data always increases the variance of an estimator. The contradiction that arises when a Bayesian credible interval includes the null hypothesis while a frequentist confidence interval does not.

37 What is the primary application of "Gumbel distribution" in statistical modeling?

Modeling symmetrically distributed continuous data. Modeling extreme value events, such as maximum flood levels or longest droughts. Modeling count data with many zeros. Modeling the survival times of patients in clinical trials.

38 What is the "Efron's bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap" method specifically designed for?

To produce point estimates that are unbiased. To provide more accurate and robust confidence intervals, especially when the sampling distribution of the statistic is skewed or biased. To reduce the computational cost of standard bootstrapping. To perform hypothesis testing without requiring distributional assumptions.

39 What is the main characteristic of "robust standard errors" (e.g., Huber-White or sandwich estimators) in regression?

They assume that the error terms are perfectly normally distributed. They provide consistent estimates of standard errors even when the assumption of homoscedasticity is violated. 40 In Bayesian inference, what defines a "proper prior" compared to an "improper prior"?

A proper prior integrates to a finite value (e.g., 1), while an improper prior does not. A proper prior is always uniform, while an improper prior is always informative. 41 What is the primary purpose of a "Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)" in causal inference?

To summarize descriptive statistics of a dataset. To visually represent assumptions about causal relationships between variables, aiding in identifying confounding and deriving identification strategies. To model time-series dependencies. To perform cluster analysis.

42 What is "uniformity" as a desirable property of a statistical test?

The test statistic always follows a uniform distribution. The power function of the test is constant across all possible alternative hypotheses. 43 What is "super-efficiency" in asymptotic estimation, and why is it usually considered problematic for regular estimators?

An estimator that is always more efficient than the maximum likelihood estimator. An estimator that achieves a variance lower than the Cramer-Rao lower bound at a specific parameter value, but not uniformly, potentially causing issues for regular estimators. An estimator that converges to the true parameter value very slowly. An estimator that is completely robust to outliers.

44 In structural equation modeling (SEM), what does the "identification problem" refer to?

The difficulty in identifying the correct model among several competing models. The inability to uniquely estimate all model parameters from the observed covariance matrix. The problem of identifying outliers in the dataset. The challenge of assigning observed variables to latent constructs.

45 What is the "Birnbaum's Theorem" a cornerstone for in foundational statistics?

46 What is the primary distinction between "Mixture Models" and "Latent Class Analysis (LCA)"?

47 What is the fundamental concept behind "optimal stopping problems" in sequential analysis?

48 What is the "Frisch-Waugh-Lovell Theorem" useful for in linear regression?

49 What is the main idea behind "Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)" as a non-parametric method?

50 What is "Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA)" designed to address?

The issue of multicollinearity in regression. The need to perform hypothesis testing without a null hypothesis. The computational complexity of MCMC methods.

51 What is the primary characteristic of a "martingale" in probability theory?

52 What is the "Lindley's Paradox" (or Jeffreys-Lindley Paradox) concerned with?

The observation that frequentist p-values and Bayesian posterior probabilities can diverge significantly for precisely specified null hypotheses, especially with large sample sizes. 53 In causal inference, what is the role of the "collapsibility" assumption for effect measures?

It states that the crude (unadjusted) effect measure is equal to the adjusted effect measure when conditioning on a covariate. It ensures that the effect of a treatment is always positive. 56 What is the role of "Stein's Lemma" in decision theory and estimation?

It provides a method for constructing uniformly most powerful tests.

57 In survival analysis, what is the purpose of a "competing risks model"?

To model the occurrence of multiple distinct events where the occurrence of one prevents the occurrence of another (or changes its probability). 61 What is the role of "sufficient statistics" in relation to the "Rao-Blackwell Theorem"?

The Rao-Blackwell Theorem states that if an unbiased estimator exists, it can be improved (in terms of variance) by conditioning on a sufficient statistic. 62 What is the purpose of the "Hausman test" in econometrics for panel data models?

63 What does "strict stationarity" imply for a time series?

64 What is the concept of "local robustness" versus "global robustness" for estimators?

65 In Bayesian inference, what defines a "reference prior"?

A prior chosen to be uniform across all possible parameter values. An improper prior designed to be as non-informative as possible in a specific sense, often derived from maximizing expected Shannon information. 66 What is the "General Method of Moments (GMM)" primarily used for in econometrics?

67 What is the primary advantage of "Quantile Regression" over Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression?

It allows for estimating the effects of predictors on different quantiles (e.g., median, 25th percentile) of the response variable, not just the mean, and is robust to outliers. 68 What is the "Kolmogorov's Axioms" foundational for in probability theory?

They specify the conditions for a hypothesis test to be valid.

69 What is "information geometry" a field of study for in statistics?

70 In causal inference, what does a "synthetic control method" aim to achieve?

To randomly assign a control group for an intervention. To construct a synthetic counterfactual for a treated unit by creating a weighted average of control units, especially useful for single case studies or few treated units. To control for all observed confounders using matching. To perform a meta-analysis of multiple intervention studies.

71 What is the purpose of "regularization" in high-dimensional settings, beyond preventing overfitting?

To ensure all coefficients remain large. To address issues of multicollinearity and high variance in coefficient estimates when the number of predictors approaches or exceeds the sample size. To reduce the computational cost of model fitting. To guarantee that the residuals are normally distributed.

72 What is the "Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem" a fundamental result for?

It defines the conditions under which a sufficient statistic exists. It provides a necessary and sufficient condition for a statistic to be sufficient for a parameter. It is used for deriving the maximum likelihood estimator. It establishes the properties of uniformly most powerful tests.

73 What is the purpose of "variance stabilizing transformations" in statistical modeling?

To convert a non-linear relationship into a linear one. To transform data so that the variance becomes constant across different levels of the mean, often improving the validity of assumptions in parametric tests. To normalize the distribution of the dependent variable. To reduce the number of outliers in a dataset.

74 What does the "Principle of Equivariance" refer to in estimation theory?

An estimator is equivariant if it is robust to outliers. An estimator is equivariant if its behavior is consistent under certain transformations of the data or parameters. An estimator is equivariant if its expected value is equal to the true parameter. An estimator is equivariant if it always has the minimum variance.

75 In multivariate statistics, what is "Discriminant Analysis" primarily used for?

To reduce the dimensionality of data by identifying latent factors. To predict group membership for observations based on a set of predictor variables, by finding linear combinations that best separate groups. To identify correlations between two sets of variables. To cluster observations into homogeneous groups.

76 What is the fundamental concept of "exact tests" (e.g., Fisher's Exact Test or exact permutation tests)?

They provide p-values that are approximations based on asymptotic distributions. They provide p-values that are computed exactly based on permutations of the observed data, without relying on asymptotic approximations or distributional assumptions. They are only applicable to continuous data. They require very large sample sizes to be valid.

77 What is "cross-sectional dependence" in panel data models, and why is it a concern?

It means that observations across different units (e.g., countries, firms) are correlated at a given point in time, violating independence assumptions and potentially biasing standard errors. It implies that the dependent variable is related to the independent variables. It is a benign characteristic of panel data that simplifies analysis.

78 What is the "Pitman-Koopman Theorem" famous for in statistical theory?

It identifies the family of distributions for which sufficient statistics of fixed dimension exist, essentially the exponential family. It proves the existence of maximum likelihood estimators. It describes the properties of Bayesian credible intervals. It establishes the conditions for a time series to be stationary.

79 In Bayesian computation, what is the key distinction between "Gibbs sampling" and "Metropolis-Hastings algorithm"?

Gibbs sampling requires sampling from full conditional distributions, while Metropolis-Hastings can use arbitrary proposal distributions, accepting/rejecting samples. Metropolis-Hastings is only used for discrete parameter spaces. Gibbs sampling does not require computing likelihoods.

80 What is the "Wilks' lambda" statistic primarily used for in multivariate analysis?

To test for the homogeneity of variances across groups. To test the equality of means across multiple groups for multiple dependent variables simultaneously in MANOVA. To measure the correlation between two sets of variables. To assess the goodness-of-fit for a structural equation model.

81 What is the definition of "asymptotic normality" for an estimator?

82 What is the "likelihood ratio principle" a fundamental method for constructing in hypothesis testing?

Non-parametric tests. Optimal tests, especially when uniformly most powerful tests do not exist, based on comparing the maximum likelihood under the null and alternative hypotheses. Bayesian credible intervals. Descriptive statistics.

83 What is the primary characteristic of a "doubly robust" estimator in causal inference?

It provides consistent estimates if either the outcome model or the propensity score model is correctly specified, but not necessarily both. It always has a smaller variance than other estimators. It combines two different statistical tests into one.

84 What is the "concentration parameter" (or dispersion parameter) in the context of the Dirichlet distribution?

85 What is the "bootstrap percentile-t method" designed to achieve?

To provide exact p-values for permutation tests. To construct confidence intervals based on bootstrap distributions, particularly for quantities whose sampling distribution is skewed, by using studentized statistics. To reduce the computational cost of bootstrapping. To estimate the parameters of a time series model.

86 In structural equation modeling, what are "modification indices" used for?

To suggest potential improvements to a model by indicating how much the chi-square statistic would decrease if a currently fixed parameter were freely estimated. 87 What is "information projection" (or I-projection) used for in information theory and statistics?

To find the probability distribution that is "closest" to a given distribution within a specified family, minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence. To project data points onto a linear subspace. To visualize complex statistical relationships.

88 What is "exchangeability" in the context of Bayesian hierarchical models?

The assumption that all parameters are independent. The assumption that the units (e.g., individuals, groups) are interchangeable in their probabilistic behavior before observing the data, implying that their joint distribution is invariant to permutation. The ability to exchange prior distributions for different parameters. The property that the mean and variance are equal.

89 What is the "Hoeffding's inequality" a bound for?

The difference between the sample mean and the population mean for independent bounded random variables. The maximum possible correlation between two variables. The minimum variance of an unbiased estimator. The probability of a Type I error.

90 What is the main characteristic of "kernelized support vector machines (SVMs)" for classification?

They assume a linear decision boundary in the original feature space. They implicitly map data into a higher-dimensional feature space using kernel functions to find non-linear decision boundaries. They are primarily used for regression tasks. They require the data to be perfectly normally distributed.

91 What is "Mendelian randomization" designed to achieve in epidemiological studies?

To randomly assign genetic interventions to participants. To investigate causal relationships between an exposure and an outcome using genetic variants as instrumental variables to overcome confounding and reverse causation. To identify genetic markers associated with disease. To estimate the heritability of complex traits.

92 What is the "Profile Likelihood" approach used for in parameter estimation?

To estimate all parameters simultaneously in a complex model. To obtain confidence intervals or test hypotheses for a parameter of interest when other nuisance parameters are present, by maximizing the likelihood over the nuisance parameters for fixed values of the parameter of interest. To transform a likelihood function into a posterior distribution. To assess the goodness-of-fit for a model.

93 What is the primary purpose of "factor analysis" beyond simple dimensionality reduction?

To predict a dependent variable from a set of independent variables. To identify underlying latent constructs (factors) that explain the correlations among a set of observed variables. To classify observations into distinct groups. To model time-series dependencies.

94 What is the "marginal structural model (MSM)" approach designed to address in causal inference with time-varying confounding?

To estimate causal effects in cross-sectional data. To estimate the causal effect of a time-varying treatment on an outcome, controlling for time-varying confounders that are themselves affected by past treatment. To identify instrumental variables for complex interventions. To perform mediation analysis for static exposures.

95 What is the concept of "local false discovery rate" (local FDR) in multiple hypothesis testing?

The probability that a false positive occurs among all rejected null hypotheses. The probability that a specific null hypothesis is true, given that it has been rejected, offering a more intuitive measure than the p-value. The expected proportion of false discoveries among all discoveries. The Type I error rate for a single test.

96 What is the role of "sufficient statistics" in relation to the "Fisher-Neyman Factorization Theorem"?

The theorem proves that every distribution has a sufficient statistic. The theorem states that a statistic is sufficient if and only if the likelihood function can be factored into two parts, one depending on the data only through the statistic and the other not depending on the parameter. The theorem demonstrates that sufficient statistics are always unbiased. The theorem specifies how to combine multiple sufficient statistics.

97 What is the characteristic feature of the "Laplace approximation" in Bayesian inference?

It provides an exact analytical solution for complex posterior distributions. It approximates a posterior distribution with a Gaussian distribution centered at the mode, often used when MCMC is too slow or complex. It is a non-parametric method for density estimation. It is used for testing hypotheses about means.

98 What is the "difference-in-differences (DiD)" estimator primarily used for in quasi-experimental designs?

To compare the means of two groups at a single time point. To estimate the causal effect of an intervention by comparing the change in outcomes over time in a treated group to the change in outcomes over time in an untreated control group. To perform a meta-analysis of observational studies. To identify instrumental variables.

99 What is the meaning of "unbiasedness" in the context of estimating equations (e.g., GEE)?

The estimator always hits the true parameter value. The expected value of the estimating equation, evaluated at the true parameter, is zero. The estimating equations are always linear. The estimating equations are always robust to outliers.

100 What is the "Kalman filter" specifically designed to achieve in time series analysis?

To forecast future values of a stationary time series. To provide optimal (minimum mean square error) estimates of the unobserved state of a dynamic system from noisy measurements. To detrend and deseasonalize time series data. To perform spectral analysis on time series.

101 What is the distinction between "marginal independence" and "conditional independence" in probability?

Marginal independence means two variables are independent, while conditional independence means they are independent given a third variable. Marginal independence applies only to discrete variables, conditional independence to continuous. Conditional independence always implies marginal independence. Marginal independence is a stronger condition than conditional independence.

102 What is "conjugate analysis" a benefit of in Bayesian inference for posterior calculations?

It always leads to improper posterior distributions. It simplifies the calculation of the posterior distribution by ensuring that the prior and posterior belong to the same distributional family. It reduces the need for prior information. It ensures that the posterior distribution is always centered around the sample mean.

103 What is the purpose of the "optimal design of experiments" framework?

To randomly assign treatments to maximize generalizability. To select experimental settings (e.g., sample sizes, treatment levels) that maximize the information gained about parameters of interest, often by optimizing the Fisher information matrix. To minimize the cost of data collection, irrespective of information gain. To ensure all confounding variables are accounted for.

104 What is the "bootstrap hypothesis testing" method typically used for?

To perform exact tests without any assumptions. To construct p-values for hypothesis tests by resampling under a specific null hypothesis (e.g., by recentering the data) without relying on parametric assumptions. To estimate the parameters of a specific distribution. To calculate confidence intervals for known parameters.

105 What does the "Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test" address?

It compares the means of three or more groups. It assesses the association between two categorical variables, controlling for the effect of a third categorical confounding variable (stratification). It tests for overall significance in a regression model. It detects autocorrelation in time series data.

106 What is the concept of "model calibration" in predictive modeling?

The process of adjusting model parameters to improve overall accuracy. The assessment of how well a model's predicted probabilities match the observed event frequencies. The selection of the optimal set of features for a model. The training of a model on new, unseen data.

107 What is the role of the "Score function" in maximum likelihood estimation?

It measures the goodness-of-fit of the model. It is the first derivative of the log-likelihood function with respect to the parameters, and its expectation is zero at the true parameter values, crucial for estimation and inference. It defines the Hessian matrix. It is used to calculate the observed Fisher information.

108 What is "concentration inequality" (e.g., Chernoff bound, Hoeffding's inequality) primarily used for in theoretical statistics?

To determine the exact probability distribution of a random variable. To provide probabilistic bounds on how much a random variable deviates from its expected value. To calculate the exact confidence interval for a parameter. To prove the consistency of an estimator.

109 What is the main characteristic of "kernel methods" in machine learning and statistics?

They assume linearity in the original feature space. They implicitly map data into higher-dimensional feature spaces using kernel functions, allowing for non-linear relationships to be modeled with linear algorithms. They are only applicable to discrete data. They require explicit computation of high-dimensional feature vectors.

110 What is the "generalized method of moments (GMM)" especially powerful for in econometrics?

When the full likelihood function of the data is known and easily maximized. When the econometric model has more moment conditions than parameters, allowing for over-identification tests. For estimating parameters in a simple linear regression model. For analyzing time series data with clear seasonal patterns.

111 What is the role of "sufficiency" and "completeness" for a statistic in estimation theory?

Sufficiency means it captures all information for a parameter, completeness means it's the minimal such statistic. Sufficiency means it reduces variance, completeness means it ensures unbiasedness. Sufficiency means it is asymptotically normal, completeness means it is consistent. Sufficiency means it's always unique, completeness means it's always non-biased.

112 What is the "Wald's identity" in sequential analysis?

It provides a formula for the expected value of the sample size in sequential hypothesis tests. It relates the expected value of the sum of a random number of random variables to the expected value of the number of variables and the expected value of each variable. It defines the conditions for a random variable to be independent. It establishes the asymptotic normality of maximum likelihood estimators.

113 What is the "marginal posterior distribution" in Bayesian inference?

The posterior distribution of all parameters in the model simultaneously. The posterior distribution of a subset of parameters, obtained by integrating (marginalizing) over the nuisance parameters. The prior distribution before observing any data. The likelihood function for the observed data.

114 What is the concept of "identifiability" in mixture models?

The ability to identify the correct number of components in the mixture. The ability to uniquely determine the parameters of each component distribution and their mixing proportions from the overall mixture distribution. The ease with which the model can be interpreted. The process of identifying which data points belong to which component.

115 What is the "Kolmogorov complexity" (or algorithmic information theory) a measure of?

The complexity of a statistical model's formula. The shortest possible computer program that produces a given string or object, representing its intrinsic informational content. The computational time required to fit a statistical model. The difficulty of interpreting the results of a statistical analysis.

116 What is the "Granger causality test" used for in time series analysis?

To determine if one time series consistently precedes another. To test whether past values of one time series variable provide statistically significant information about future values of another time series variable, beyond what is provided by its own past values. To identify common trends in multiple time series. To remove seasonal components from a single time series.

117 What is the characteristic of "Huber loss" (or M-estimation) in robust regression?

It uses the squared error loss for all residuals, making it sensitive to outliers. It is quadratic for small residuals and linear for large residuals, providing a compromise between OLS and least absolute deviations regression, making it more robust to outliers. It completely ignores large residuals. It always leads to coefficients being exactly zero.

118 What is "Bayesian nonparametrics" primarily concerned with?

Using parametric models with very simple prior distributions. Using flexible stochastic processes (e.g., Dirichlet processes) as priors over function spaces or infinite-dimensional parameter spaces to avoid rigid parametric assumptions. Performing hypothesis testing without any prior information. Analyzing categorical data using Bayesian methods.

119 What is the main application of "copula functions" in multivariate statistics?

To model linear correlations between variables. To model the dependence structure between random variables independently of their marginal distributions. To transform non-normal variables into normal ones. To perform principal component analysis on non-Gaussian data.

120 What is the "Godfrey-Breusch test" used for in regression analysis?

To test for heteroscedasticity in the residuals. To test for autocorrelation in the residuals of a regression model, especially higher-order autocorrelation. To detect multicollinearity among independent variables. To assess the normality of residuals.

121 What is "Fisher's consistency" a property of an estimator?

The estimator converges to the true parameter as the sample size increases. The estimator is asymptotically unbiased. The estimator, when applied to the full population distribution, yields the true parameter value. The estimator has the minimum possible variance.

122 What is the "Wald-Wolfowitz runs test" used for?

To compare the means of two independent samples. To test the randomness of a sequence of binary outcomes or continuous data dichotomized by the median, by counting consecutive identical observations (runs). To detect heteroscedasticity in regression residuals. To assess the goodness-of-fit for a continuous distribution.

123 What is "semiparametric regression" characterized by?

Models that assume a fully known parametric form for all components. Models that combine parametric and non-parametric components, often assuming a parametric form for the regression coefficients but a non-parametric form for the baseline function or error distribution. Models that exclusively use non-parametric methods. Models that always produce exact p-values.

124 What is the "Kolmogorov-Smirnov test" for two samples primarily used for beyond simple mean comparison?

To test if two samples come from the same population distribution, without assuming a specific distribution shape. To compare the variances of two independent groups. To detect autocorrelation in a time series. To assess the goodness-of-fit for a linear regression model.

125 What is the concept of "admissibility" for an estimator in decision theory?
